stem:
In thale cress, Arabidopsis thaliana, most of the stomata are on the lower surface of the leaves.
Fig. 4.1 is a diagram of an open stoma and two guard cells. Some of the cellulose fibres in the cell wall of the guard cells are shown.
{{figure:figure_4_1.webp}}
Fig. 4.1

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The cellulose fibres shown in Fig. 4.1 are composed of bundles of cellulose microfibrils.
Explain how molecules of cellulose are arranged into a microfibril.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem: The width of stomatal openings in A. thaliana is regulated by movement of ions. These ions move through channel proteins in the cell surface membranes of the guard cells.
parts.text:
Draw a diagram to show part of a cell surface membrane with a channel protein.
Label your diagram.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why channel proteins are needed for the movement of ions into and out of cells.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The outward movement of ions from guard cells causes stomata to close.
A variety of A. thaliana does **not** have channel proteins for the outward movement of ions in the cell surface membranes of the guard cells.
Suggest **and** explain the effect of **not** having these channel proteins on transpiration.
